system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a male with hepatitis C-related cirrhosis and multifocal hepatocellular carcinoma, was admitted for post-procedural observation following his fourth transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) for residual liver tumors. The procedure was performed successfully under image guidance, targeting tumors in multiple liver segments using Oncozene beads. He tolerated the intervention well with no immediate complications and remained stable throughout the brief admission. His cirrhosis, diabetes, coronary disease, and other comorbidities were managed with continuation of home medications, including diuretics, antivirals, nadolol, and rifaximin. He was monitored for post-embolization syndrome but required no pain medication. Antibiotic prophylaxis was administered, with a course of oral ciprofloxacin prescribed at discharge. He was discharged home in good condition with instructions to monitor for fever or pain, continue all medications, and follow up with his liver specialist in two weeks.
problems: Unspecified viral hepatitis C without hepatic coma
Cirrhosis of liver without mention of alcohol
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Coronary atherosclerosis of unspecified type of vessel, native or graft
Family history of ischemic heart disease

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  HCC.  Reviewed in liver tumor conference ___

COMPARISON:  Comparison is made to MR abdomen performed for ___.

TECHNIQUE:   OPERATORS: Dr. ___ radiology fellow) and Dr.
___ radiology attending) performed the procedure.   Dr.
___ radiologist, personally supervised the trainee during the key
components of the procedure and reviewed and agreed with the trainee's
findings.

ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
125 mcg of fentanyl and 2.5 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of 105 min during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine
was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.

MEDICATIONS: Fentanyl, Versed, lidocaine, 30 mg of Toradol, 3 g of Unasyn

CONTRAST: 110 ml of Optiray contrast.

FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  32.9 min, 464 mGy

PROCEDURE:  1. Right common femoral artery access.
2. Common hepatic arteriogram with cone beam CT.
3.  Right hepatic arteriogram.
4.  Right hepatic arterial embolization with doxorubicin-loaded Oncozene
drug-eluting beads.
5.  Left hepatic arteriogram with cone beam CT.
6. Right common femoral arteriogram
7. Deployment of Angio-Seal arterial closure device

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent for the procedure and
chemotherapy was obtained from the patient/from the healthcare proxy/using an
interpreter.  The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed
supine on the exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___
protocol.  Both groins were prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.

Using palpatory and fluoroscopic guidance, the right common femoral artery was
punctured using a micropuncture set at the level of the mid-femoral head. A
0.018 wire was passed easily into the vessel lumen. A small skin incision was
made over the needle. Then the inner dilator and wire were removed and a
___ wire was advanced under fluoroscopy into the aorta. The micropuncture
sheath was exchanged for a 5 ___ sheath which was attached to a continuous
heparinized saline side arm flush.

A C2 glide Cobra catheter was advanced over ___ wire into the aorta. The
wire was removed and the celiac artery was selectively cannulated and a small
contrast injection was made to confirm position.  The Cobra catheter was
advanced into the common hepatic artery over a glidewire. The glidewire
removed and hand injection of dilute contrast confirmed positioning. A common
hepatic arteriogram was performed. A STC microcatheter pre-loaded with a
double angled wire was used to access the right hepatic artery and a right
hepatic hand injection arteriogram was performed.  Second order right hepatic
arterial embolization was performed with approximately 35% of the 100 mg of
dose of doxorubicin-loaded onto 1 vial 100 micron Oncozene drug-eluting beads.

The micro catheter was withdrawn and the Cobra catheter was advanced into the
left hepatic artery over the glidewire. Hand injection dilute contrast
confirmed position. Left hepatic arteriogram with cone beam CT was performed.
The STC microcatheter pre-loaded with a double angle wire was then used to
access the left hepatic artery.  Attempts to advance the wire into the third
order left hepatic artery thought to be partly supplying the right hepatic
dome lesion was unsuccessful and the further attempts to treat this branch was
aborted.

CONE-BEAM CT:  First, a rotational cone beam CT was performed with the
catheter in the common hepatic artery, to delineate the hepatic arterial
anatomy and blood supply to the tumor.  Multiplanar CT images were
reconstructed and 3D volume-rendered images of the arterial anatomy required
post-processing on an independent workstation by the attending physician, ___.
___.  After the initial superselective treatment of the Segment VIII lesion,
a second cone-beam CT was performed from the LHA.  This was done as the
initial cone-beam CT and angiogram suggested that some additional tumor supply
arose from a small branch of the LHA but the exact feeding branch could not be
definitely identified.  The cone-beam CT was essential in evaluating LHA
supply to the Segment VIII tumor.  Multiplanar CT images were reconstructed
and 3D volume-rendered images of the arterial anatomy required post-processing
on an independent workstation by Dr. ___.  These images were used in the
interpretation and reporting of this procedure.

All materials used in chemotherapy delivery were disposed of per departmental
protocol. A common femoral arteriogram was performed prior to use of a closure
device. Manual pressure was held until hemostasis was achieved.

The patient tolerated the procedure well.

FINDINGS: 

1. Conventional hepatic arterial anatomy .
2. Pre-embolization arteriogram showing tumor blush in hepatic segment VIII.
3. Cone-beam CTs showing hepatic segment VIII tumor predominately supplied by
the right hepatic artery though there is question of additional left hepatic
arterial supply
4.  Post-embolization showing staining of tumors in hepatic segment VIII.
5. Left hepatic arteriogram and cone beam CT demonstrating tiny additional
supply to hepatic segment VIII tumor
6. Right common femoral arteriogram demonstrating anatomy compatible with
arterial closure device

IMPRESSION: 

Successful right common femoral artery approach trans-arterial
chemoembolization of hepatic segment VIII tumor.

RECOMMENDATION:  Followup imaging in 1 month.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. You've just come back from your TACE procedure, and I wanted to check in on how you're feeling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, doctor. I’m feeling okay—no pain or anything. A little tired, but that’s about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. The team said the procedure went well. They targeted a tumor in segment VIII of your liver using chemo-embolization through the right hepatic artery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was it the same spot as before? I remember last time was tough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This is a different area—segment VIII, which showed up on your recent MRI. It’s about 2.7 cm and met criteria for treatment. They used doxorubicin-loaded beads to target it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did they get all of it? I’m worried it might come back again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The imaging shows successful embolization. There was a small possible supply from the left hepatic artery, but it was very minor and not treatable this time. The main feeding vessel was fully treated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. Do I need a CT scan after this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No CT needed this time. The real-time imaging during the procedure confirmed good delivery. You’ll have a follow-up MRI in about a month to check the response.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in again. Any nausea, fever, or pain since the procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, still feeling fine. My leg where they went in feels okay—no bleeding or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. The closure device worked well, and your pulse is strong down there. We’re keeping an eye out for post-embolization syndrome, but so far, so good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs came back. Your blood counts are stable—white count and platelets are low but unchanged from before. Liver enzymes are slightly up, which is expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a problem? My numbers are always a bit off because of my liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Given your cirrhosis, these are actually reassuring. Your glucose is better today—147—down from 226 yesterday. Probably because you were fasting for the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been watching my sugar, but it’s hard sometimes. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on all your usual meds—furosemide, spironolactone, nadolol, rifaximin, and your diabetes pills. We’re adding a nausea medicine—prochlorperazine—just in case you feel queasy over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And I should call if I get a fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—any fever over 100.4, significant pain, or nausea you can’t control, please call your liver team. Otherwise, keep your follow-up appointment in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you’re feeling well and your vitals stay stable. You’re alert, walking fine, and your exam looks good. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did great with the procedure. Just take it easy for a few days, stick to your meds, and we’ll see how the next scan looks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my leg swelling seems a bit worse. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You do have mild increase in your right leg edema, likely from a bit of salt in your diet before admission. Keep taking your diuretics and monitor it. If it gets much worse, let your doctor know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll watch it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. You’re all set to be discharged. Someone will bring your prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. See you next time.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a male with hepatitis C-related cirrhosis and multifocal hepatocellular carcinoma, was admitted for post-procedural observation following his fifth transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) for a 2.7 cm tumor in hepatic segment VIII. The procedure was successfully performed via the right hepatic artery using doxorubicin-loaded Oncozene beads, with minor additional supply noted from the left hepatic artery that was not amenable to treatment. He tolerated the intervention well without immediate complications, remained hemodynamically stable, and reported no pain, nausea, or procedural site issues. His cirrhosis, diabetes, and other comorbidities were managed with continuation of home medications. A mild increase in right leg edema was noted, attributed to dietary salt intake. He was discharged home the following day in stable condition with instructions to monitor for fever or pain, continue all prescribed medications, and follow up with his liver team in two weeks for evaluation and planning.
